There are still quite a few branches in the "tech tree". There are some docs here: https://github.com/ethereum/stateless-ethereum-specs <GuthL> 👍 Any write-up regarding Verkle trees? it does not need to be a write-up, just a gist of it maybe, to start with. Because I have no idea at all 🙂 to start with, why they are called "verkle" is it this: https://math.mit.edu/research/highschool/primes/materials/2018/Kuszmaul.pdf ? just googled it <@!364458974906548225> I've been told that after I had to leave, you asked for details on my work on the binary conversion. Here you are: * ethresearch post: https://ethresear.ch/t/overlay-method-for-hex-bin-tree-conversion/7104 * EIP: https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/2584 * blog post: https://medium.com/@gballet/ethereum-state-tree-format-change-using-an-overlay-e0862d1bf201 Thanks <@!353136597522448385> , I just looked at the last link, and it is now much more clear to me (after 30 seconds of reading 🙂 ) how the overlay transition would work > it does not need to be a write-up, just a gist of it maybe, to start with. Because I have no idea at all 🙂 <@456226577798135808> I did a post a while back on adapting pointproofs for witness compression https://ethresear.ch/t/adapting-pointproofs-for-witness-compression/7363. It is similar to the idea in the link you posted. Keen to see how this is related to what <@!273808422753796097> and others have in mind. just a quick question: these point proofs. Given commitment to a vector `v` of `n` values, say `C(v)`, does a point proof prove that `v[i]=x` for given `i`, `x` and `C(v)`? I think this is great! What I would suggest as the next step for these proposals (both your article and Verkle tree article), from my point of view is the system for maintaining the tree of those ranges, over which you are generating point proofs. My intuition tells me that something akin of B+-tree would be the structure that can accomplish that. because there is a trade-off here, between size of the "page" being too large to make re-doing vector commitments too costly, and too small to have to change too many of them upon the state modification > just a quick question: these point proofs. Given commitment to a vector `v` of `n` values, say `C(v)`, does a point proof prove that `v[i]=x` for given `i`, `x` and `C(v)`? <@456226577798135808> Yes, as well as for multiple points like i1, i2 ... ik valuating to x1... xk, one point would prove that. The proofs can be aggregated to one point across commitments. This is similar to polynomial commitments. I am planning to add a response to that post, comparing polynomial commitments. Also, I haven't actually elaborated on the limitation of Verkelizing these vector commitments. I plan to do that as well. https://notes.ethereum.org/@afhGjrKfTKmksTOtqhB9RQ/rkWVGPP6L ^ Call transcript; digest in a few <vbuterin> <@689635476826619924> "No exclusion proofs. Hence this approach is not applicable for data availability and accumulator problems." is a showstopper <vbuterin> Unfortunately we need to seamlessly handle the case where a not-yet-existent object gets accessed I am revisiting Vitalik's post/presentation on the polynomial commitments, because now I finally started to have a capacity to understand it 🙂 <vbuterin> So a quick update on where we've thought since then: * It turns out that while updating the *commitment* after a state update is easy, updating *witnesses* is hard. You pretty much need to do O(N) work to recompute all the witnesses * A reasonable max state size to target would be something like 2**36 to 2**48, and even the aggressive lower bound is larger than any reasonable trusted setup. Hence, we need some kind of multi-layer structure. * And it turns out that multi-layer structures make witness updates easier! Hence our interest in verkle trees now I see. Yes, when I saw in the verkle paper that the generation of proofs is expensive for large vectors, I automatically thought of B-trees 🙂 <vbuterin> right now I am trying to think and see if there's a way to make a key/value map in the polynomial commitment context without doing a hashmap or a tree structure 😢 question to that: would the proofs aggregate well across different components of such multi-layer structure? Or does the aggregation only work within one "page" ? <vbuterin> Aggregation does indeed work across different components <vbuterin> So a proof consists of all intermediate commitments, plus one single witness <vbuterin> See https://github.com/ethereum/research/blob/master/verkle/verkle.py for an implementation ok > <vbuterin> Unfortunately we need to seamlessly handle the case where a not-yet-existent object gets accessed. > <@!273808422753796097> I don't understand yet, why exclusion proofs are necessary for plain witness compression <vbuterin> witnesses are going to sometimes access accounts or storage slots that are not-yet-existent btw <@456226577798135808> do we have an idea of what percentage of storage or account accesses are to blank slots / empty accounts? not on top of my head (I never asked myself this question), but I think I can get some answer in couple of days <vbuterin> This could help us as there's a tradeoff in that schemes get easier to build if it's ok to make exclusion proofs more expensive

excerpts.author: eth2_gitter_bot
excerpts.content:
<vbuterin> So a quick update on where we've thought since then:
* It turns out that while updating the *commitment* after a state update is easy, updating *witnesses* is hard. You pretty much need to do O(N) work to recompute all the witnesses
* A reasonable max state size to target would be something like 2**36 to 2**48, and even the aggressive lower bound is larger than any reasonable trusted setup. Hence, we need some kind of multi-layer structure.
* And it turns out that multi-layer structures make witness updates easier!
Hence our interest in verkle trees now
